cues.text: MIT 8105, Network Architecture and Protocols.
This is Study Session 01: Foundations of Network Architectures and Design Principles.
We begin with the first chapter, Networks from first principles.
Let us start with the most basic question: what is a computer network?
A computer network connects devices so that they can exchange information and share resources, and they do this according to protocols.
A protocol is simply an agreed set of communication rules.
Without those shared rules, two devices could be physically wired together and still be unable to understand each other.
Now let us meet the building blocks.
End devices are the devices that originate data or consume it.
Think of a laptop sending a request, or a phone displaying a web page.
A NIC, a network interface card, attaches a device to the transmission medium, which is the cable or radio channel carrying the signals.
A switch forwards frames within a LAN.
A router forwards packets between IP networks.
Notice the precise terms: switches deal in frames inside a local network, while routers deal in packets moving between different IP networks.
An access point connects wireless stations to a distribution network, which means it is the bridge between Wi-Fi devices and the wired infrastructure behind them.
A firewall enforces traffic policy, deciding which traffic is allowed and which is not.
Two more roles to distinguish.
Servers provide services, while clients request them.
A web server serves pages, and your browser, acting as a client, asks for them.
Then there are a few older or more specialised devices.
A hub repeats bits to all of its ports.
Unlike a switch, it does not learn MAC addresses, so it cannot be selective about where traffic goes.
A modem adapts signals for a particular access medium, converting between what the device produces and what the medium can carry.
And a gateway connects systems, or serves as a route to another network.
Next, networks are classified by their scale.
A LAN, a local area network, covers a local site.
A WLAN is a wireless LAN.
A PAN, a personal area network, covers personal devices, such as your phone and earbuds.
A CAN, a campus area network, links nearby buildings.
A MAN, a metropolitan area network, spans a metropolitan area.
A WAN, a wide area network, connects geographically dispersed locations.
Beyond these size categories, we have some related terms.
The Internet is a network of interconnected networks.
An intranet is a private organisational network.
An extranet grants controlled external access to selected outsiders, such as partners or suppliers.
We also distinguish two architectural styles.
In client-server architectures, services and administration are centralised.
In peer-to-peer architectures, roles are distributed among peers.
This can reduce central dependency, because no single machine is essential, but it can complicate governance, since control and policy are spread out and harder to manage.
Now let us look at how data actually travels.
Data is represented as bits, and those bits are carried by electrical, optical or radio signals.
Different media suit different needs.
Twisted pair is economical for local Ethernet.
Fibre offers long reach and electromagnetic immunity, meaning it is not disturbed by electrical interference.
Wireless supports mobility, but it shares spectrum and encounters interference.
Three performance terms are often confused, so keep them apart.
Bandwidth is capacity.
Throughput is the achieved data rate, what you actually get.
Latency is delivery delay, how long data takes to arrive.
Transmission can be serial or parallel.
Serial transmission sends bits sequentially, one after another.
Parallel transmission sends multiple bits simultaneously across multiple paths.
We also describe the direction of communication in three modes.
Simplex is one-way, and the example given is a broadcast-only sensor, which only sends.
Half-duplex allows both directions, but not simultaneously, like a walkie-talkie, where you must take turns.
Full-duplex allows simultaneous transmission and reception, and the example is modern switched Ethernet.
Finally, consider who a message is addressed to.
Unicast is one sender to one receiver.
Broadcast reaches all members of an IPv4 broadcast domain.
Multicast reaches subscribed groups, meaning only those that have asked to receive it.
Anycast routes a packet to one member of a set, usually selected by routing.
An important point on IPv6: it has multicast and anycast, but not broadcast.
This leads us to address resolution.
ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol, resolves IPv4 neighbour addresses to link-layer addresses.
To do this, it broadcasts requests on the local segment, essentially asking everyone nearby which device owns a given IPv4 address.
Since IPv6 has no broadcast, it does things differently: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery.
